title: Prices for gear upgrades: a share of band gold, or typed
question: On 2026-11-18 you kept typed Hallmark prices on purpose (150,000, 250,000, 400,000 and 600,000 for tiers 4 to 7), and said upgrades should cost more than a hero can afford in a band so players choose what matters. The book's GR-8 prices Tempering, Hallmarks and linings as a share of a band's gold, so a band's upgrades total 1.2 to 1.4 of what the band earns. You let it stand on the page in about a second (reversal row 6). The first build keeps your typed prices. The rest of the overhaul must pick one. Which?

options.label: A share of band gold
options.text: Every standing upgrade costs a share of the band's simulated gold, so the 1.2 to 1.4 holds at every Level and no price goes stale as Levels climb. MEASURED on run 44920906999, before the engine fix: full best gear costs about 0.18 of a band's net gold for a lone hero, far under the size you asked for. Cost: your four typed Hallmark numbers are replaced by shares, and every price is as true as the calibration of the simulator's gold (chapter 14, section 2). The screen can still say a price in gold and in hours of hunting.

options.label: Typed, re-sized
options.text: Prices stay typed numbers, written by the designer for each tier so a band's upgrades total 1.2 to 1.4 of its simulated gold, and re-typed when each region is written. Cost: your four Hallmark numbers still change, because they sit under the size you asked for. A typed table grows with every band and goes stale if the gold a band earns moves, which the formula brief asks to avoid. JUDGMENT.

options.label: Your numbers as typed
options.text: Your four Hallmark numbers stand exactly, and later tiers get typed numbers in the same spirit. Cost: COMPUTED from the measurement in a, a band's upgrades cost a small part of what it earns, so the choice between upgrades that you asked for on 2026-11-18 does not bite until prices rise. With upgrades this cheap every player fills them, so the sinks you meant on 2026-11-18 as the place where bought gold becomes an edge hold little.

title: The yard's rate
question: Three times (2026-11-14, and twice on 2026-11-20) you kept a flat yard rate, with the screen saying what an hour buys. The book's GR-54 makes the yard's XP an hour follow the skill curve, capped at half of what hunting pays that skill, with the fee following the rate. You let it stand on the page in about a second (reversal row 11). The first build keeps the flat rate and the fee you ruled, 100 gold times the skill level an hour. Which is the yard?

options.label: Follows the skill curve
options.text: The yard pays a share of each skill level's cost and never more than half of what hunting pays that skill. Its size is set in the simulator against the town-hour model. Cost: it reverses your three rulings. JUDGMENT from the book: skill levels cost more as they climb, so any flat rate is too strong early and worth almost nothing late.

options.label: Flat, as ruled
options.text: The yard pays a flat XP an hour and the screen says what an hour buys, as you ruled. The fee stays 100 gold times the skill level an hour. Cost: JUDGMENT from the book: early the flat hour can be worth more than hunting gives that skill, and late it is worth little, so the yard matters in a middle stretch. UNKNOWN where that stretch sits until the town-hour model runs.

options.label: Flat, set per band
options.text: A flat rate that the designer types once for each skill band from the simulator, so the screen still names a plain number and the rate keeps some worth at every band. Cost: a typed table that grows with every band, which the formula brief asks to avoid. JUDGMENT.
